questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I'd lived in South America before so I wanted to go back to be able to enjoy more of the language, culture and beautiful nature there:)

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had an amazing trip overall! A few reasons why it isn't a 10 is that Bogotá is a huge and overwhelming city + there's a lot of insecurity that you need to consider.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy! Not all of it made sense immediately, but -NAME REDACTED- is the person in charge of the exchange program, and any question or doubt I had I'd just ask him, and he'd help me figure it out.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: -NAME REDACTED- - he was pretty quick at responding and would help out with any doubts you had.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found the whole housing situation a bit overwhelming to figure out from home, so I booked an Airbnb for the first month (could probably just have done 2 weeks), and then my plan was to figure it out when I got there. I met two really nice girls during the summer course, and ended up moving in together with them in CentralX - so it all worked out great:)

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: There are various options! I personally lived in CentralX which was fine but not amazing. It's not super expensive (compared to cph) and the reception makes it feel pretty safe. However, there's no stuff in the apartments so you need to buy basics for the kitchen, duvet, pillows, bedsheets and stuff like that + it is a bit of a soulless place made for rich 17-year olds who's moved out for the first time. Other options are staying in CityU (would not recommend, you can't even open the windows) or moving in to some of the bigger houses a bit further away from uni.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Courses are first come, first served so you should sign up as soon as the sign up-process opens - though it opens up for exchange students and first year students a bit earlier than for everyone else. The course registration happened online in two separate programs (which was a bit confusing). They explained it multiple times, but I never really understood how it worked hahah. I did the summer spanish course tho which means I was already in Bogotá when we had to sign up for courses, and they hosted a session where we could show up and get help. -NAME REDACTED- helped me then and honestly I don't know if I would've figured it out on my own...

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: -NAME REDACTED- is the main help available in general! If you're already in Bogotá you can show up to the session they host, and if you're not I think there was a teams chat where you could ask questions and then -NAME REDACTED- would reply pretty quickly.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I wanted!

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You can't apply for courses that happen at the same time, so having planned out what courses you want to apply to and alternatives if you don't get these courses is a good idea + apply for more courses than you need cause you can always drop them later!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found the level to be quite low compared to UCPH and the contents of the classes weren't very complicated. The only thing that surprised me was how much time a had to spend doing various assignment during the semester - it's definitely a lot more work, although then there's barely an exam period then, which makes it kinda worth it.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Usually at UCPH I have a mix of seminars and larger lectures (all voluntary) and what is being taught is based on a book. At UniAndes they only have more seminar style classes (where you can't have more than 20% absence), and the courses mainly center around what the professor says. In some of the classes there was external material but I didn't find it super relevant to the classes, so I didn't really read it. The exams and general evaluation (spread between many different assignments) are all elaborated and evaluated by the professor.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Propiedad Industrial, Derecho e Industria Cultural, Ética Profesional and Derecho Internacional II

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I liked Derecho e Industria Cultural + it didn't demand too much during the semester.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Travelling can be pretty expensive! I'm used to Copenhagen being more expensive than the rest of Denmark, but Bogotá isn't super touristy, so the more touristy places (e.g. Medellín and Cartagena) are a lot more expensive! Flights can also be pretty expensive, and it's not always advised to take the bus (both with regards to time and security).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I mainly used Uber/InDrive to get around - it's very cheap, but since it's the main form of transportation it adds up. If you want to buy any food that's not typically colombian (e.g. tinned tomatoes or coconut milk) it's super expensive! Eating out is really cheap though.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were lots of clubs, sports classes and general activities. I didn't join a club, but I used the pool quite a bit + did salsa and yoga classes.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Have a look at what's there and maybe try something new! Try the salsa class (also just to get to experience Mauricio hahah:))

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I'd never been to Colombia before so I did kind of a classic tourist route (with a few not so touristy places); Cartagena, Medellín, Cali, Desierto de Tatacoa, Villa de Leyva. Some of my friends, that had already been, went less well-known places and had a great time. I also went to Peru and saw Machu Picchu over the longer break:)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Colombian people are super welcoming which helps with the culture shock, but I still struggled a bit with the things that are just inherently different - just a matter of getting used to it tho:)

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk to people in your classes! People are really super nice and open + there's a lot of group work where so it's nice to know some people, and if you don't you'll get to meet them there!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I look very european so people would stare a lot, point at me and talk to me on the street. Sometimes I'd have nice chats with people, but sometimes I just wanted to be anonymous and be left alone hahah

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How lovely the people are! They are so proud of their country, and they want to share the best parts of their culture, like food, music, dance, with you.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Travel! Colombia has so much to offer, and one semester is not enough to get to see everything. I feel like I've only seen a small part of the country, but my most important take away is that I'll definitely come back
2. Do the 3 week summer spanish course! We were around 30 people, whereas there are like 250-300 people starting when the semester starts so it's a bit easier to get to know people. I met my closest friends there:)
3. Be aware, but don't be afraid. You definitely need to consider security, but I made it through without anything happening, so it is possible!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: It's useful to know at least a bit of spanish before going. I spoke pretty fluently and still struggled sometimes - both at uni and out in the real world. If you study law, there are also barely any classes in english, which means you might have to do classes in spanish. Other than that speaking spanish just opens so many doors to be able to get to know Colombia and Colombians:)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know Colombia - beautiful country with lovely lovely people! Also the friends I made on exchange, very excited to hang out with them again in Europe!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Probably always feeling like (and being treated like) a foreigner because of how different I look and act

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go - you're not going to regret it!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
